lines: Here's a pipeline that looks, from the outside, completely healthy.
Every single task in last night's run reported success. Nothing paged. And yet the table a stakeholder reads from was still stale when they opened it this morning.
So the pipeline wasn't actually lying to anyone. It was just never asked the one question that mattered.
Before I tell you what that question is, commit to an answer yourself.
The pipeline already had three numbers sitting there: whether every task succeeded, how many rows got written, and how old the newest partition actually is.
Which one of those three would have told you, in the middle of the night, that something was wrong?
answer: Task success doesn't do it, because a task can exit cleanly while doing essentially nothing useful.
Row count doesn't do it either. A job can rewrite yesterday's same rows every single night and report a perfectly healthy count.
Only the age of the newest partition measures what a reader actually experiences, regardless of what the task itself believes happened.

lines: That gap starts with how you even write down what happened.
A sentence in a log file is something a human has to read and interpret. A structured record just carries the same named fields every single time: which run, which task, which asset, which partition.
That one small discipline is what makes everything after it possible.
Here's what that discipline is actually worth.
Mix four separate runs together into one pile of log lines, and a human is stuck reading every one of them to find the run they care about.
Ask the same question of the structured version, by that one key, and you get back only the records that actually belong to your run. Nothing else.
Now, not every number behaves the same way, and picking the wrong shape for one will bite you later.
Rows processed only ever climbs. It's a running total, and the only thing that can bring it back down is the process itself restarting.
That's the entire contract of what's called a counter: up, or back to the start. Nothing in between.
A queue, on the other hand, genuinely falls. Things get drained out of it, not just added.
Try to force that falling number through something that only knows how to increase, and watch what happens to a real queue that drained down to seventy.
The honest answer a counter can give you isn't seventy. It's zero, because resetting is the only decrease it has.
Task duration is a different shape of problem entirely, because it isn't one number at all. It's a whole distribution of them.
A histogram handles that by sorting observations into buckets and keeping a running sum alongside them.

But read a percentile back out of those buckets and remember what you're holding: an estimate interpolated between bucket edges, not an exact figure, and definitely not something you can average across two separate machines.
Put four of those pieces together and you get six signals worth watching on any pipeline.

Three carry straight over from any web service: how fast, how often it fails, how much is flowing through. Three are specific to a pipeline: how far behind a consumer is, how big a backlog has grown, and how fresh the data actually is.

That last one is the one with no equivalent anywhere else. A request-response service has nothing like it. And it's the one that would have caught last night's failure instantly: a partition that sat over ten hours old while every task bar on the dashboard stayed green the entire time.
Getting that number out of the pipeline is its own small problem, because of how it gets collected.
A scraper that checks in every fifteen seconds simply never catches a job that starts and finishes in four. It isn't unlucky. It's structurally impossible for it to see.
Pushing the value in instead solves that, but be careful: a gateway built for pushing keeps repeating that same old number forever, long after the job that sent it is gone, unless someone deletes it.
One more thing worth trying before you call any of this done: add a single label splitting that same counter by customer.
It looks like a small, reasonable addition. It is not. Each distinct customer now gets its own separate series, stored and queried independently.
Ten customers, ten series. Ten thousand customers, ten thousand series, out of what used to be one.
So here's everything this pipeline now actually has to say about itself.
A record carries its own fields and its own key. Each number gets the metric shape it actually behaves like. Six signals are watched, one with no equivalent outside a pipeline.
And every one of those signals got there by being pushed or pulled, deliberately, not by accident.
One more to actually commit to, because this is the test that matters.
A brand new stage gets added to this pipeline. It has no instrumentation yet, it runs faster than any reasonable scrape interval, and three other jobs read whatever it writes.
Is wiring up throughput and error rate enough, or is there something else this stage needs before you'd trust it?
answer: Throughput and error rate only tell you the job ran and didn't crash. That's exactly the all-green picture from the very start of this topic.
What's missing is freshness: whether what it wrote is actually new, pushed at the end of each run, because nothing running faster than the scrape interval can be reliably pulled.
Skip that, and you've built the same silent failure you opened this topic with, just one stage further down the pipeline.
